Cautiously supportive tone: The FOMC notes a strong labor market and robust household spending, but weakness in business fixed investment and exports alongside sub-2% inflation and low market-based inflation compensation. The literature suggests investment is central to business-cycle dynamics and often drives GDP fluctuations in downturns; firms’ investment and inventories are sensitive to financing conditions and internal funds (e.g., Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein 1994; investment spending often accounting for declines in real GDP). By cutting the funds rate to 1.50–1.75% and using T-bill purchases and repo operations to keep reserves ample, policy can ease financing constraints and support capex via the credit/liquidity channel. With inflation expectations anchored, New Keynesian Phillips-curve evidence (Galí, Gertler, and López-Salido; Rudebusch) implies muted inflation response to slack, which—together with a below-target inflation shortfall—supports easing consistent with Taylor-style reaction principles (Taylor 1983; McCallum and Nelson 1999). Empirical VAR work (Sims; Zha) documents real effects of monetary shocks, reinforcing the case that the action can cushion downside risks. Net: slightly positive but risk-aware.
